name: Pathology Detection and Scan Triage
title: Pathology Detection and Scan Triage
answer: Pathology detection and scan triage covers software that examines medical images for signs of disease or injury and software that orders the resulting worklist. Detection tasks include lung nodules on chest CT, fractures on plain radiographs, intracranial hemorrhage on head CT, and breast lesions on mammography. Triage tasks flag urgent studies, such as a suspected large vessel occlusion or a tension pneumothorax, and move them to the top of a radiologist's queue. The scope also includes the quality checks and worklist rules that decide which studies the model sees and how its output is presented. This site tracks 1000 medical AI models, and a meaningful share of them sit in this area.

sections.body: Pathology detection and scan triage covers software that examines medical images for signs of disease or injury and software that orders the resulting worklist. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on a mix of on-premises GPU servers, private cloud, and edge devices inside the imaging department. They connect to the picture archiving and communication system, or PACS, and to the radiology information system through standards such as DICOM and HL7. Inference usually happens close to the scanner or on a dedicated server so that a study can be processed in seconds to minutes. Storage and network capacity matter because a single CT or MRI series can contain hundreds of images. Some vendors offer a container or virtual appliance that the hospital installs behind its firewall, while others provide a cloud service with a local cache.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with a curated dataset of images and labels, often annotated by subspecialty radiologists who mark lesions or assign a triage category. Developers train deep learning models, commonly convolutional neural networks or vision transformers, to produce a detection score, a segmentation mask, or a priority level. Validation uses held-out retrospective data and, increasingly, prospective silent trials where the model runs alongside clinical care without changing it. Reported metrics include sensitivity, specificity, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, positive predictive value, and time to report for flagged cases. In deployment, the model receives a DICOM series, applies preprocessing, runs inference, and writes a result back to the worklist or a viewer, where a radiologist remains responsible for the final read.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk begin with the provenance of training data, including consent, de-identification, and the terms under which images were collected. Regulatory clearance, such as FDA authorization or CE marking, defines the intended use and the claims a vendor may make. Liability questions are active: this site tracks 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, and those cases shape how vendors write contracts and how hospitals assess coverage. Clinical risks include false negatives that delay care, false positives that cause unnecessary follow-up, automation bias, and alert fatigue when too many studies are flagged. Provenance also covers model versioning, audit logs, and the ability to reproduce a result months after a study was read.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward foundation models that can handle multiple modalities and tasks with less task-specific training. Triage is expanding from single-condition alerts to multi-condition worklist optimization that accounts for scanner capacity, subspecialty schedules, and patient flow. Prospective randomized studies and post-market surveillance are becoming more common as payers and regulators ask for evidence of clinical benefit. Integration is shifting from a separate AI viewer to embedded results inside the primary reading environment. The site tracks 215 compliance and regulation pages, a sign of how much of the work now sits in documentation, monitoring, and change control.
